Place a pencil at a slant in the glass of water and look down from above: it seems bent or broken near the surface, and its submerged end appears slightly raised (Figure 151).
From the side of the glass, the submerged part seems shifted sideways and appears wider in diameter (Figure 152).

Refraction can make an object's size, shape, and position appear different.
A simple observation shows this effect.

Place a coin or another small object at the bottom of an empty glass, then move the glass until the coin's center, the rim, and your eye lie on one straight line.
Keep your head in the same position while adding water: as the water level rises, the bottom and the coin seem to rise slightly, and a coin that was only partly visible becomes fully visible.

These effects can be explained by light changing direction at the boundary between two media.
The ray traveling through the first medium toward the boundary is the **incident ray**.

Draw a line perpendicular to the boundary through the point of incidence: this is the normal; the angle $\alpha$ between the incident ray and the normal is the **angle of incidence**.
The ray in the second medium is the **refracted ray**, and its angle $\beta$ with the normal is the **angle of refraction** (Figure 153).
